Loans and mortgages, in one place

Most of us have more than one kind of borrowing. Each kind affects the others.

If you take on a car loan, a mortgage lender will usually offer you less. If you remortgage, the cost of your other borrowing can shift too. The 23 UK calculators on this site are free, and they're built to show you those connections. Your numbers stay on your own screen.

Start with the question most people get wrong

If you're weighing up borrowing, the number in front of you is usually the monthly payment, because that's the number lenders advertise. It's the wrong number to decide on. A longer term lowers the monthly payment and raises the total cost, every single time.

Guides that join the two up

Every guide here is about the place where unsecured borrowing meets a mortgage. Those are the questions a loans-only or a mortgages-only site can't answer.

How Your Loans Cut What You Can Borrow

Every £100 a month you're paying towards loans or cards takes roughly £5,000-£7,000 off what a mortgage lender will offer you. Here's the arithmetic they use, and what you can do about it.

Consolidating Debt Into Your Mortgage

If you move unsecured debt onto your mortgage, the monthly payment comes down and the lifetime cost usually goes up. It also turns debt you couldn't lose your home over into debt you can.

Total Cost, Not Monthly Payment

Choosing borrowing by the monthly figure quietly costs people more than almost any other habit in personal finance. This guide shows you what to compare instead.

Deposit, or Clear the Debt First?

If you've got a lump sum, and both a loan and a house deposit to think about, which pound works harder depends on three things. One of them isn't the interest rate.

Your Credit File Before a Mortgage Application

A mortgage underwriter reads things on your file that a loan underwriter doesn't. This guide covers those, along with why the timing of your applications matters, and the searches that quietly count against you.

Secured or Unsecured: What Actually Changes

The rate difference is the part everyone sees. What matters more is what the lender can do if you stop paying.
